discovery: Deterministic single-photon and indistinguishable-photon sources based on semiconductor quantum dots
motivation: Around 2000, İmamoğlu, Michler and Yamamoto showed that a single semiconductor quantum dot, driven by optical or electrical pulses, can act as a triggered source that emits exactly one photon at a time. Yamamoto's group then showed that successive photons from such a dot are indistinguishable, which is what two-photon interference requires. İmamoğlu and Michler showed triggered single-photon emission from quantum dots in microcavities. Their work turned artificial atoms in solids into on-demand quantum light sources. Quantum-dot sources now combine near-unity purity and indistinguishability with high brightness. They power boson-sampling and photonic quantum-computing experiments, quantum key distribution and entanglement distribution, and they are made commercially. This work founded solid-state quantum photonics and made the single photon an engineered, practical resource for quantum technologies.
